summary: An island country in the western Pacific off East Asia, officially named the Republic of China. It has been ruled by the Dutch, the Ming loyalist Zheng regime, the Qing dynasty and Japan, completed its democratization in the 1990s, and is known for its semiconductor industry and night-market culture.

ranking.name: Folk religion
ranking.description: Beginning in the 17th century, large numbers of migrants from Zhangzhou and Quanzhou in Fujian and from Guangdong risked crossing the "Black Water Ditch" (the Taiwan Strait) to Taiwan, bringing deities such as Mazu, the Wang Ye (Royal Lords) and Tudigong (the Earth God) to pray for a safe passage and successful land reclamation, and villages often formed around temples. The Kominka (imperialization) movement of the late Japanese period, from 1937, consolidated temples, but belief revived quickly after the war. Today events such as the Dajia Mazu pilgrimage draw hundreds of thousands of participants; many people do not consider themselves to belong to any particular religion yet worship deities and ancestors in daily life and at festivals, so folk religion is the most widespread form of belief.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism arrived with migrants during the Zheng era and the Qing period and often blended with folk religion; during the Japanese period, Japanese Buddhist schools also established temples in Taiwan. In 1949 large numbers of monks came from mainland China, and from the 1960s groups such as Fo Guang Shan (1967), Tzu Chi (1966), Dharma Drum Mountain and Chung Tai Chan Monastery promoted "Humanistic Buddhism," attracting many urban followers through education, medical care and disaster relief, making Buddhism one of the most influential organized religions in Taiwan.

ranking.name: Taoism
ranking.description: Taoism arrived with Fujianese and Cantonese migrants; Taoist priests preside over rituals such as jiao offerings and rites of exorcism for temples, and the relationship with folk religion is so close that the two are often hard to distinguish clearly. In 1949 the 63rd Celestial Master, Zhang Enpu, came to Taiwan with the government, making Taiwan an important base for the Zhengyi (Orthodox Unity) tradition. Many temples are registered as Taoist, so there is a great deal of overlap between Taoists and followers of folk religion in the statistics.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After the war, Taiwan went through rapid industrialization, urbanization and the spread of higher education, and the proportion of younger people taking part in religious activities has fallen markedly. Because folk religion has no initiation ritual, many people who worship at festivals or honor their ancestors choose "no religion" in surveys, so this share also reflects the loose and diverse character of belief in Taiwan.

ranking.name: Christianity (including Catholicism)
ranking.description: When the Dutch East India Company ruled southern Taiwan from 1624 to 1662, missionaries of the Reformed Church preached to the Siraya people; in 1859 the Dominican Order of the Catholic Church returned to Taiwan. In 1865 James Laidlaw Maxwell of the English Presbyterian Church practiced medicine and preached in Tainan, and in 1872 George Leslie Mackay of the Canadian Presbyterian Church founded a church and school in Tamsui, with far-reaching effects on medicine and education. After the war, large numbers of indigenous people converted to Christianity, and their proportion of believers is much higher than that of the Han Chinese, though Christianity remains a minority nationwide.

religion.background: The indigenous peoples of Taiwan originally worshipped ancestral spirits and nature spirits. Dutch and Spanish rule in the 17th century brought Christianity, and at the same time large numbers of Fujianese and Cantonese migrants came to Taiwan, bringing Buddhism, Taoism and a folk religion represented by Mazu and Tudigong. During the Japanese period, Japan promoted Shinto and Japanese Buddhism, and the Kominka movement after 1937 further suppressed traditional temples. After 1949, mainland migrants brought still more religious organizations, and after martial law was lifted in the 1980s religious freedom flourished, producing today's religious landscape in which Buddhism, Taoism and folk religion are intermingled and many religions coexist.

language.official: The National Language Development Act (2019) stipulates that the natural languages used by all of Taiwan's indigenous ethnic groups, together with Taiwanese Sign Language, are national languages.

ranking.name: Mandarin
ranking.description: Mandarin (Guoyu, the "national language") became the official language after the Nationalist government took over Taiwan in 1945; a National Language Movement was promoted from 1946, and after 1949 large numbers of mainland migrants also came to Taiwan. Schools long banned dialects and punished violators, and the media restricted broadcasting time in local languages, making Mandarin the common language among ethnic groups. Today the great majority of the younger generation speak Mandarin as their first language, and almost everyone in the country understands it.

ranking.name: Taiwanese Hokkien (Tâi-gí)
ranking.description: Taiwanese Hokkien derives from the Southern Min brought by migrants from Quanzhou and Zhangzhou after the 17th century; the accents of the two places blended in Taiwan, giving rise to the so-called "Zhang-Quan mixture," and it also absorbed vocabulary from the Pingpu languages and Japanese. After the war, the National Language Movement and the 1976 Radio and Television Law, which restricted dialect programs, reduced the use of Taiwanese; after martial law ended in 1987, the nativization movement drove a revival of Taiwanese, and the 2019 National Language Development Act officially designated it a national language. It is still the everyday language of many households in central and southern Taiwan.

ranking.name: Hakka
ranking.description: Hakka was brought by Hakka people who migrated to Taiwan from the 18th century onward from the Jiaying, Huizhou and Chaozhou areas of Guangdong, and is mainly distributed in Taoyuan, Hsinchu, Miaoli and the Liudui region of Pingtung. After the war, the Mandarin-only policy caused serious loss of Hakka; the 1988 "Return Our Mother Tongue" movement became an important milestone for language rights, and Hakka TV began broadcasting in 2003. Although Hakka people make up more than about 10 percent of the population, those who use Hakka as their main language have become quite few.

language.history: The languages of Taiwan's indigenous peoples belong to the Austronesian family, and scholars generally believe that Taiwan may be one of the homelands of the Austronesian peoples. From the 17th century, Hokkien and Hakka migrants came to Taiwan in large numbers, and Hokkien became the most widely spoken language. During the Japanese colonial period (1895-1945), Japanese-language education was promoted; after the war the Nationalist government pursued the National Language Movement, suppressing local languages. After martial law was lifted in 1987, a local-language revival movement arose, and the 2019 National Language Development Act designated the languages of all of Taiwan's indigenous ethnic groups, as well as Taiwanese Sign Language, as national languages.

ranking.name: Beef noodle soup
ranking.description: A red-braised broth simmered for a long time from beef, beef bones, doubanjiang (chili bean paste), soy sauce and spices, served with large chunks of beef shank and noodles, topped with pickled mustard greens and chopped scallions.
ranking.history: In Taiwan's agricultural society of the past, many people did not eat beef because the ox was an important source of labor. After 1949, large numbers of Nationalist soldiers and their dependents came to Taiwan with the government; it is generally believed that Sichuanese veterans in the military dependents' villages of Gangshan, Kaohsiung, used locally produced doubanjiang in beef noodle stew, developing "Sichuan-style red-braised beef noodle soup," which then spread to Taipei and gave rise to many beef noodle shops. In 2005 Taipei City began holding a Beef Noodle Festival, and beef noodle soup went from a military dependents' village flavor to a representative Taiwanese dish.

ranking.name: Bubble tea (pearl milk tea)
ranking.description: Black, chewy tapioca pearls made from cassava starch are added to sweetened black tea or milk tea, which is shaken, served cold and sipped through a wide straw.
ranking.history: In the 1980s, bubble tea shops (foam black tea shops) rose in Taiwan, and both Chun Shui Tang in Taichung and Hanlin Tea Room in Tainan claim to have been the first to add tapioca pearls to milk tea; the two have even fought a trademark lawsuit over it. Tapioca pearls were originally an ingredient in traditional Taiwanese sweet soups, and cassava starch was a starch once produced in large quantities in Taiwan. From the 1990s, bubble tea spread across Asia with Taiwanese tea-drink chains, and after the 2000s it swept Europe and America, becoming one of Taiwan's best-known exports of food culture.

ranking.name: Braised pork rice (lu rou fan)
ranking.description: Pork with skin is cut into small cubes or minced, braised for a long time with soy sauce, rock sugar, shallots and five-spice, and ladled over white rice; it is salty, sweet and rich.
ranking.history: Braised pork rice derives from the Hokkien home-style method of braising pork; in times of scarcity, braising cheap pork skin and scraps into a sauce for rice let a family eat their fill with plenty of rice-friendly flavor. Fried shallots are the soul of Taiwanese braised pork rice and also a hallmark of Hokkien cuisine. After the war, as the economy developed, braised pork rice went from a home-cooked dish to the signature of snack stalls and lunchbox shops; its price is modest, and it remains one of the most commonly eaten everyday foods among Taiwanese.

ranking.name: Oyster omelette (o-a-tsian)
ranking.description: Fresh oysters are fried on a griddle with sweet potato starch batter, eggs and greens into a pancake and topped with sweet and spicy sauce; it is crisp outside, chewy inside and tastes of the sea.
ranking.history: Oyster farming has flourished along Taiwan's southwestern coast since the Qing dynasty, and oysters were an inexpensive seafood easily obtained locally, while sweet potato starch was a product of the sweet potatoes widely grown in Taiwan in the past. One popular story holds that when Koxinga attacked Taiwan in 1661 his army ran short of provisions and soldiers fried pancakes of oysters and sweet potato starch to stave off hunger, but this is only a legend with no historical records to prove it. The oyster omelette later became a representative snack at the night markets of Tainan and Taipei, and similar dishes exist in Fujian, Chaoshan and the Chinese communities of Southeast Asia.

ranking.name: Stinky tofu
ranking.description: Tofu is soaked in a brine fermented from vegetables, bamboo shoots, fish and shrimp, then deep-fried, steamed or stewed in a spicy broth; it smells bad but tastes good.
ranking.history: Stinky tofu originated in China; folk legend says it was invented by accident by Wang Zhihe, a Qing-dynasty juren scholar from Anhui, and different methods later developed in different places. After the war, mainland migrants brought this kind of fermented tofu to Taiwan, where deep-fried stinky tofu served with Taiwanese-style pickled cabbage developed, along with the spicy stinky tofu of the Shenkeng area. It is the most representative "strong-flavored" snack at the night markets and is often the first challenge for foreign visitors trying Taiwanese food.
